about: Every headline claim this project makes, and what would fail if it were false. Not every sentence - the load-bearing ones, the ones a reader would quote. Defect §15 is why this file exists: two claims were graded PROVEN on evidence that did not support them, and nothing in the repository connected a claim to the test that was supposed to defend it.

grades.PROVEN: a test in this repository fails if this stops being true, AND a negative control shows the test can fail
grades.ADAPTER-PROVEN: the code is right; says nothing about any deployment or any database
grades.SKIPPED: not checked on a default run. Never reported as a pass
grades.DELEGATED: outside what the engine can see. The caller answers it
grades.NOT-CLAIMED: the arithmetic does not support it and no document asserts it

rules.everyClaimNeedsATest: A claim with no `test` is a claim nobody is defending. PROVEN and ADAPTER-PROVEN require one.
rules.provenNeedsANegativeControl: A PROVEN claim needs something deliberately broken that the test rejects - a mutant, a fake, or a mutation entry. Otherwise it is §15: a test that passes and could not fail.
rules.numbersMustBeGenerated: A numeric claim must name the command that produces it. `pnpm audit:claims` enforces that the command EXISTS and is a real package script; `pnpm verify:numbers` re-runs a registered subset of facts and fails when a document states a different value. Until v1.0 this rule claimed that audit:claims re-ran and compared - it did not, and five deliberately-broken numbers passed it. See DEFECTS_FOUND.md §18. Facts outside verify:numbers' list are still unchecked prose.
rules.notClaimedNeedsNoTest: NOT-CLAIMED and DELEGATED claims are about what is NOT asserted. The prose guard defends those, not a unit test.

claims.claim: The policy engine is pure: no imports, no clock, no randomness, nothing async.
claims.negativeControl: mutation entry `core-purity`: adding a node:fs import to policy.ts must fail the contract test
claims.note: The import half of this check was VACUOUS from the day it was written until v1.0 - the stripper blanked string literals before the scan, so it matched nothing. See DEFECTS_FOUND.md §16.

claims.claim: The 16 v0 holdout cases have not changed, byte for byte.
claims.negativeControl: a formatter rewrote three files once and `pnpm verify:corpus` caught it against corpus/holdout/MANIFEST.sha256 - defect §5

claims.claim: 62 imported cases rebuild byte-identically from committed upstream source rows.
claims.negativeControl: editing one imported string makes the rebuild diverge and `pnpm import:check` exits 1; the rebuild runs from scripts/import-injecagent.mjs

claims.claim: A receipt admits one value, into one slot, once - and a label-only receipt matches nothing where the label repeats.
claims.negativeControl: mutant M9 argname_only_binding, bitten by corpus slot-t-001 and nothing else

claims.claim: When the guard loses a receipt race it re-decides rather than returning the stale verdict.
claims.negativeControl: a store that reports unspent on read and already-taken on write
claims.note: Graded PROVEN in v0.9 on a test that could not fail. Deleting the branch left 74/74 passing. See DEFECTS_FOUND.md §15.

claims.claim: Every capability table in this repository has zero structural contradictions.
claims.negativeControl: packages/core/test/manifest.test.ts constructs contradictory manifests and asserts each code fires; neutralising any validatePolicy rule fails a named test

claims.claim: Every mutant is bitten somewhere and none is bitten everywhere; the reference is bitten by nothing.
claims.negativeControl: `pnpm report:mutants` exits 1 if any mutant is bitten by nothing or by everything - the bite matrix is built in scripts/bite-matrix.mjs

claims.claim: 99 of 99 silent attacks are contained; the classifier catches 0.
claims.negativeControl: NONE THAT IS A DELIBERATELY BROKEN ARTIFACT. The cited labelling-convention assertion is a second assertion over the same data, not a control - flagged by adversarial review at v1.0. What holds the number honest is that `pnpm report` recomputes it from the corpus on every run and verify:numbers fails if a document disagrees.
claims.note: Downgraded from PROVEN at v1.0. The measurement is real and regenerated, but PROVEN in this registry requires a negative control showing the test CAN fail, and this claim never had one. See DEFECTS_FOUND.md §19.

claims.claim: The policy engine special-cases no business domain: no refund, ticket, deploy, kubernetes, invoice, solana or USDC anywhere in packages/core/src, with one asserted exemption - toolrisk.ts, an advisory naming heuristic that decide() does not import, may contain the verbs deploy and refund.
claims.negativeControl: appending `export const LEAK = "kubernetes"` to packages/core/src/check.ts fails "the engine contains no domain vocabulary"; demonstrated, and it PASSED before v1.0 widened the scan from policy.ts to the whole package
claims.note: Stated precisely because the first version of this entry said "no wallet" - which is FALSE: `wallet` appears four times in policy.ts, because `wallet_sign` is a capability name, and it was never in the scanned word list. The claim is about the engine not branching on a DOMAIN, not about the absence of a substring. `wallet_sign` names a capability class - irreversible, full egress, nothing lifts it - and its BEHAVIOUR is domain-independent; only its name is not. Caught by an adversarial audit of this registry. See DEFECTS_FOUND.md §17. v1.0: an adversarial reviewer showed the entry said "anywhere in its code" while the test read ONE file - `export const X = "deploy"` in check.ts passed 461/461, and `deploy` and `refund` were ALREADY live in the shipped toolrisk.ts. The scan now walks every file in the core package and the toolrisk exemption is pinned by a second test that fails if decide() ever imports it. See DEFECTS_FOUND.md §19.

claims.claim: No document asserts a freeze proof, calls Postgres proven without its condition, implies a validated manifest is honest, claims the workflows prove judgement, or asserts optimality.
claims.negativeControl: an injected false claim is demonstrably caught by `pnpm audit:docs`; the five prose rules live in packages/conformance/test/claims.test.ts

claims.claim: Concurrent reserve, cross-process replay refusal, restart durability, crash handling and bounded stale reclaim hold against a real Postgres.
claims.negativeControl: a read-then-write adapter in the same script must double-claim
claims.note: SKIPPED is the honest grade for a DEFAULT run: nothing runs this without DATABASE_URL and CI never sets one, which is precisely what this registry defines SKIPPED to mean. On a run WITH DATABASE_URL the script proves all five scenarios and the read-then-write control double-claims; that run is real and reportable, but it is not what `pnpm test` or CI does. Graded PROVEN until v1.0, when an adversarial reviewer pointed out the entry contradicted the registry's own vocabulary. See DEFECTS_FOUND.md §19.

claims.claim: The reserve/decide/consume-or-release protocol never spends a receipt behind a refusal.
claims.negativeControl: a read-then-write async adapter fails exactly one conformance scenario under `pnpm prove:asyncledger`

claims.claim: The sync cross-host claim is earned by passing five interleavings, not asserted.
claims.negativeControl: nonAtomicStore fails exactly the concurrent double-spend scenario under `pnpm prove:crosshost`

claims.claim: Without DATABASE_URL the real-database proof reports SKIPPED / NOT PROVEN and exits 0.
Whether your hosts point at one database is a question the caller answers.
Whether a capability declaration is honest cannot be established from the declaration.
No policy here is proven optimal. Five profiles, two undominated.
That the holdout predates the engine is UNAVAILABLE, not pending.
A tool declared weaker than it is lets 21 of 30 direct-harm and 32 of 32 data-stealing imported attacks through.
The taint wrapper is cooperative, not enforced. There is no membrane in JavaScript.
Every registered hand-typed number in the documents agrees with the command that produces it.
claims.negativeControl: editing any registered number to a wrong value makes `pnpm verify:numbers` exit 1 - demonstrated on five facts, and it caught README.md's stale test count at v1.0
claims.note: Covers a REGISTERED SUBSET, not every number. A fact nobody listed is still unchecked prose, and the list is short and load-bearing rather than complete. v1.0 CORRECTION: this entry named packages/conformance/test/claimregistry.test.ts, which never invokes verify:numbers - so `pnpm test` passed 461/461 while the claim was FALSE (README said 454). verify:numbers shells out to `pnpm test` and therefore cannot run inside vitest; it is a CI gate, and a claimregistry test now asserts CI actually runs it. See DEFECTS_FOUND.md §19.

claims.claim: A source reached by more than one path is resolved by its own provenance, not mistaken for a cycle; a real cycle still fails closed to the top of the lattice.
claims.negativeControl: mutation entry `dag-path-scoped`: removing the path unwind and the memo from resolveTaint in packages/core/src/policy.ts must fail the diamond tests
claims.note: Graded only from v1.0.1. Before it, one seen-set was shared across a node siblings and never unwound, so an all-SYSTEM diamond resolved to UNTRUSTED_EXTERNAL. It failed CLOSED, so this was over-refusal rather than leakage. Nothing here could have caught it: no test and no corpus case declared a source with two parents. Corpus cases `dag-t-001` and `dag-t-002` are the paired positive and negative. See docs/DEFECTS_FOUND.md.

claims.claim: decide() returns a verdict for every input, including a malformed one, and never throws. Every malformed input is denied.
claims.negativeControl: mutation entry `decide-is-total`: neutralising the structural gate in packages/core/src/policy.ts must fail the totality tests
claims.note: The engine asserted this in a source comment from the day it was written, and it was false - a null input, a missing action and any non-array sources all threw. The claim sat outside the apparatus because scripts/audit-docs.mjs scans documents and this registry, never source comments. That gap is itself now covered. TypeScript does not close it: the published packages ship to consumers with no compiler in the path. See docs/DEFECTS_FOUND.md.

claims.claim: An unrecognised parameter role admits clean input only, instead of collecting the capability row loosest ceiling.
claims.negativeControl: mutation entry `unknown-role-fails-closed`: neutralising the KNOWN_ROLES check in packages/core/src/policy.ts must fail the role tests
claims.note: The one defect in this pass that could ALLOW something. ceilingFor asked whether a role was in the STEERING set; a misspelling is not in that set, so it fell through to defaultCeiling and an attacker-controlled recipient on email_send became an ALLOW purely by mislabelling the argument. Not a non-steering role and not a role at all are different facts. See docs/DEFECTS_FOUND.md.

claims.claim: A seeded search over generated provenance graphs and argument shapes finds no disagreement between the engine and an independently written taint walk, and no permitted value above its ceiling.
claims.negativeControl: the same search run against a table whose ceilings are raised, judged against the shipped ceilings, must report under-blocks; and mutation entry `dag-path-scoped` must turn this file red
claims.note: A CLEAN RUN IS A STATEMENT ABOUT THE SPACE EXPLORED, NOT A PROOF OF ABSENCE. The search generates graph shapes and argument shapes; it generates no receipts, no ledger state and no multi-step runs, and the shape vocabulary is the author’s. What it changes is that the structures are not ones anybody sat down and wrote: with defect section 23 reintroduced it finds the diamond in the hundreds within a few thousand decisions, without being handed the failing CASE - though the shape vocabulary does contain `diamond` and `stacked_diamond`, written after section 23 was known, so it was handed the failing SHAPE. Removing both of those shapes still leaves findings, by way of `fan_in`; removing every reconvergent shape leaves none. That is why the limitation in docs/LIMITATIONS.md is reduced rather than closed.

claims.claim: Coercing a Tainted value to a primitive throws instead of silently stringifying, and the label still does not survive a coercion.
claims.negativeControl: mutation entry `coercion-is-a-tripwire`: making the coercion return a string instead of throwing must fail the taint tests
claims.note: A TRIPWIRE, NOT A MEMBRANE, and the claim is worded to keep that distinction. Propagation is impossible in JavaScript - a coercion returns a primitive and a primitive cannot carry a label - and a test demonstrates it by unwrapping the hostile value and relabelling the result CLEAN. That test does NOT exercise a coercion - a coercion throws, so there is no result to inspect - and it passes with the tripwire removed. It documents the boundary; the mutation entry is what defends the tripwire itself. Section 31 recorded the earlier wording here as an overstatement and this entry reproduced it; section 33 records that. What this closes is the accidental path: template interpolation, String(), and concatenation used to produce the string [object Object] with no signal. It does nothing about map(), unsafeUnwrap(), or a value that was never wrapped. See docs/DEFECTS_FOUND.md.

claims.claim: A seeded search over receipt shapes finds no case where the engine admits an argument no valid receipt covers, and none where it refuses one that is covered.
claims.negativeControl: mutation entries `receipt-one-slot` (one receipt admitting two arguments of an action) and `slot-collision-suffixing` (two arguments declaring the same explicit path collapsing to one slot) must each fail the receipt-search tests; and the in-test control runs the engine with every ceiling raised, judged against the SHIPPED table, which must report findings. This field previously described an empty-`liftableBy` control that had already been replaced: once the search selected rows BY liftability, that control had no rows to run on and reported zero by having nothing to do. See DEFECTS_FOUND.md section 37.
claims.note: THE ADMISSION FLOOR IS THE POINT. The first version of this search never admitted a single receipt - every one used a rule its capability row does not lift by - so it explored only the refusal path while reporting what looked like broad coverage. A test now floors how many iterations reach ALLOW, because a search where no receipt ever works cannot tell a correct engine from one that refuses everything. What it does NOT cover: `spentReceipts` is a Set this process builds rather than a database, there are no multi-step runs, and it shares the lattice and the capability table data with the engine. See the receipts row of docs/LIMITATIONS.md and docs/DEFECTS_FOUND.md.
